instruction.hanzi: 听一听，读一读：下面是最常用的问候语和道歉语。
instruction.english: Listen and read along: these are the most common ways to greet someone and to apologise.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: (Ms. Liu, the teacher, comes in) Hello, everyone!

prompt.hanzi: 三人一组，分角色朗读课文，然后用自己的名字再说一遍。
prompt.english: In groups of three, read the dialogues aloud taking a role each, then do them again using your own names.
Match each line with a suitable reply.

items.hanzi: 安娜，你好！ — 马克，你好！
items.pinyin: Ānnà, nǐ hǎo! — Mǎkè, nǐ hǎo!

prompt.english: Fill in the blanks with 你, 您, 们, 不 or 关.

items.english: Your teacher greets the whole class.
Someone steps on your foot and apologises.

explanation.hanzi: 汉语的音节一般分成两部分：开头的辅音叫“声母”，后面的部分叫“韵母”。这一课先学十一个声母 b p m f d t n l g k h 和六个单韵母 a o e i u ü，再学几个复韵母。注意 b/p、d/t、g/k 的区别：p、t、k 发音时要送出一股较强的气流（送气），b、d、g 不送气。
explanation.english: A Chinese syllable usually has two parts: the consonant at the start is the "initial" (声母), and everything after it is the "final" (韵母). This lesson covers 11 initials — b p m f d t n l g k h — and the 6 simple finals a o e i u ü, plus a few compound finals. The key contrast is b/p, d/t, g/k. They are NOT voiced vs. voiceless as in English: b, d, g are plain and unaspirated (close to the p in "spy"), while p, t, k come with a strong puff of air (like the p in "pie"). Hold a sheet of paper in front of your mouth: it should flutter for p, t, k and stay still for b, d, g.

syllables: a  o  e  i  u  ü

rule.hanzi: 双唇音和唇齿音：b p m 用两片嘴唇发音；f 用上齿碰下唇。
rule.english: Lip sounds: b, p, m are made with both lips; f is made with the upper teeth on the lower lip.

examples.english: p + o (with a puff of air)

rule.hanzi: 舌尖音：d t n l 用舌尖碰上齿后面的地方。
rule.english: Tongue-tip sounds: d, t, n, l touch the ridge just behind the upper teeth.

examples.english: t + a (with a puff of air)

rule.hanzi: 舌根音：g k h 用舌头后部发音；h 比英语的 h 更有摩擦感。
rule.english: Back-of-tongue sounds: g, k, h are made at the back of the mouth. Chinese h is rougher than English h — closer to the ch in Scottish "loch".

examples.english: k + e (with a puff of air)

rule.hanzi: 单韵母：a 口张大；o 圆唇；e 不圆唇，像轻轻的“呃”；i 像 see 的 ee；u 像 food 的 oo；ü 舌头像发 i，嘴唇像发 u。
rule.english: Simple finals: a — mouth wide open, as in "father"; o — rounded lips, like "aw" with a hint of "w"; e — unrounded, a relaxed "uh" from the back of the throat; i — like "ee" in "see"; u — like "oo" in "food"; ü — say "ee" and then round your lips without moving your tongue.

examples.english: i on its own is written yi
u on its own is written wu
ü on its own is written yu
after n and l the two dots stay

rule.hanzi: 复韵母：两个元音连在一起，从第一个滑向第二个。
rule.english: Compound finals: two vowels glide smoothly into each other, with the first one stronger.

explanation.hanzi: 汉语是有声调的语言。同一个音节，声调不同，意思就不同。普通话有四个基本声调，用标在元音上的符号表示：一声 ˉ（高平），二声 ˊ（上升），三声 ˇ（先降后升），四声 ˋ（下降）。
explanation.english: Mandarin is a tonal language: the same syllable with a different pitch is a different word. There are four basic tones, marked over the vowel. Think of your voice range as five steps, 1 (low) to 5 (high). 1st tone ˉ — high and level (5-5), as if singing one note. 2nd tone ˊ — rising (3-5), like asking "What?" in surprise. 3rd tone ˇ — low dip and rise (2-1-4); start low and go lower before coming back up. 4th tone ˋ — a sharp fall from top to bottom (5-1), like a firm "No!". Say each tone with a hand gesture tracing its shape until it feels automatic.

rule.english: 2nd tone: rises from the middle to the top.

rule.hanzi: 三声：先降到最低，再升起来。
rule.english: 3rd tone: dips to the bottom, then comes back up.

rule.hanzi: 四声：从最高降到最低，又快又短。
rule.english: 4th tone: falls fast from the top to the bottom.

title.english: How a Chinese syllable is built

explanation.hanzi: 汉语的一个音节 = 声母 + 韵母 + 声调。一个汉字一般读一个音节。有的音节没有声母，只有韵母和声调，比如 ā、è、ài、ǒu。声调符号写在韵母的主要元音上。
explanation.english: Every Chinese syllable is built from three pieces: initial + final + tone. One character is (almost always) one syllable, so learning to hear these three pieces lets you spell any character you hear. Some syllables have no initial at all — just a final and a tone, such as ā, è, ài, ǒu. The tone mark always sits on the main vowel of the final. Practise by breaking the syllables below into their parts, then putting them back together.

rule.hanzi: 声调可以区别意思：声母和韵母一样，声调不一样，就是不同的字。
rule.english: Tone changes meaning: same initial and final, different tone, different word.

rule.hanzi: 声母可以区别意思：韵母和声调一样，声母不一样，也是不同的字。
rule.english: The initial changes meaning too: same final and tone, different initial.

title.hanzi: 三声变调：三声 + 三声

explanation.hanzi: 两个三声音节连在一起读的时候，第一个三声要读成二声，第二个不变。拼音里还是写两个三声符号，只是说的时候变调。“你好”写 nǐ hǎo，读 ní hǎo。
explanation.english: Saying two full dipping tones in a row is awkward, so when a 3rd-tone syllable is followed by another 3rd tone, the first one rises like a 2nd tone. The spelling does not change — pinyin still prints two 3rd-tone marks — you only change it in speech. That is why 你好, written nǐ hǎo, is actually pronounced "ní hǎo". Read the pairs below: left as written, right as said.

singleComponentChars.etymology: A single horizontal line, like one counting stick laid on a table — one of the simplest characters there is.
Two counting sticks stacked one above the other. The top line is written a little shorter than the bottom one.
Three stacked strokes, following the same tally idea as 一 and 二. The middle line is the shortest and the bottom one the longest.
In the oldest inscriptions ten was a single upright line, sometimes with a knot or dot in the middle; over time the dot stretched into a full crossbar.
Two strokes leaning away from each other, which first meant "to split apart". Its sound was borrowed to write the number eight.
Early forms look like a simple hut with a pointed roof. The word for this shape sounded like "six", so the character was borrowed for the number.

prompt.hanzi: 在教室里走一走，跟同学和老师打招呼。
prompt.english: Walk around the classroom and greet your classmates and your teacher.

activities: Greet three classmates by name: ……，你好！ — ……，你好！
Greet your teacher politely with 您好！, then let the teacher greet the whole class with 你们好！
Mini-scene: walk past a partner and "bump" into them. Apologise with 对不起！ and answer with 没关系。
Tone game: one person says mā, má, mǎ or mà; the others show the tone with a hand gesture.
